title: Three Weeks with Jesus
subtitle: Twenty-one days in the four Gospels
description: Walk with Jesus for three weeks, from the Word made flesh to breakfast on the beach. One Gospel passage a day — his birth, baptism, temptation, teaching, miracles, last supper, crucifixion, and resurrection — with a short devotional to carry it into your own day.

days.label: John 1
days.devotional: John opens his Gospel deliberately like Genesis: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' Before Bethlehem, before Nazareth, the Word was. All things were made by him, and in him was life, and the life was the light of men. Then comes the sentence that changes everything: 'And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.' The rest of the chapter gathers witnesses. John the Baptist points him out — 'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.' Andrew runs for his brother; Philip finds Nathanael; one by one they come and see. Nathanael's doubt dissolves when Jesus shows he saw him under the fig tree, and Jesus promises greater things — angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Start your three weeks here, at the doorway where eternity steps into a human life. The invitation of the whole chapter is Nathanael's: come and see.

days.label: Matthew 1–2
days.devotional: Matthew writes for readers who know their Old Testament, and he fills the birth of Jesus with it. The genealogy runs from Abraham down to 'Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.' The angel explains the name before the child is born: 'thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins' — and Matthew hears in it Isaiah's word, Emmanuel, God with us. Then come the travellers. Wise men from the east follow a star to Jerusalem, asking, 'Where is he that is born King of the Jews?' Herod is troubled, and his trouble will turn deadly. The wise men find the child, worship him, and open their treasures: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Warned in a dream, they go home another way, and Joseph escapes to Egypt by night — the family becomes refugees, then returns to Nazareth. Matthew keeps quoting the prophets as he goes, as if to say: none of this is accident. Read it slowly. God with us arrived quietly, in danger, among the poor — and exactly on schedule.

days.label: Luke 2
days.devotional: Luke tells the birth from the ground up: a decree, a journey, a stable, and a feeding-trough for a bed. But the sky does for the shepherds what it did for the wise men: 'Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.' The good news is named precisely — 'unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord' — and the sign is a baby in swaddling clothes. The shepherds make haste and find it exactly so, then go out telling everyone. In the temple, old Simeon holds the child and says the words the church still sings: 'Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation.' Anna the prophetess gives thanks and speaks of him to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. And Luke adds one line worth a book: 'And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.' The Saviour grew up — ordinary years, unnoticed obedience — before the great public days. Remember that today: faithfulness has a long, quiet middle.

days.label: Matthew 3
days.devotional: Thirty silent years end with a voice in the wilderness. John the Baptist preaches repentance, dresses like a prophet, eats like one, and will not flatter anyone — not the crowds, not the Pharisees, not Herod. His message is short: the kingdom of heaven is at hand; bring forth fruit that proves repentance. He baptizes at the Jordan, and then the moment the whole Old Testament has been leaning toward finally happens: Jesus comes to be baptized. John protests — 'I have need to be baptized of thee' — but Jesus answers, 'thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness,' standing with sinners though he had no sin of his own to confess. And heaven tears open. The Spirit of God descends like a dove, and a voice says, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' Before Jesus has preached a sermon, healed a wound, or walked on water, the Father declares his delight in him. Begin here: identity before task, beloved before busy. Whatever this week holds for you, it holds it for someone the Father has already called his own.

days.label: Matthew 4
days.devotional: Immediately after the heavens open, the desert closes in. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted, and after forty days of fasting the tempter arrives with three proposals. Turn stones to bread — satisfy yourself now, spend your power on yourself. Cast yourself from the temple pinnacle — make God prove his care with a spectacle. Fall down and worship me — take the kingdoms of the world by the shortcut. Jesus answers each one from Scripture learned in ordinary years: 'Man shall not live by bread alone'; 'Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God'; 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.' He wins not with a miracle but with obedience. Then the wilderness ends and the work begins: John is cast into prison, Jesus withdraws to Galilee, light dawns on people sitting in darkness, and his message is one word, 'Repent.' He walks by the sea and calls fishermen — 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men' — and they leave their nets the same hour. Temptation did not disqualify him; it revealed him. That pattern can be yours: victory first in small refusals, then in following.

days.label: Matthew 5–7
days.devotional: The Sermon on the Mount is three chapters, and almost every sentence is load-bearing. It opens with blessings nobody expects — the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the peacemakers, the persecuted. Then it goes to work: you are salt and light; anger is murder at the root; lust is adultery at the eye; oaths should be unnecessary because your word is true. Give without announcement. Pray simply — 'Our Father which art in heaven' — and forgive, because you have been forgiven. Do not serve mammon; the birds are fed and the lilies are clothed, and your Father knows what you need. 'Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.' Judge yourself before you judge another; ask, seek, knock; and beware of prophets who say Lord, Lord, but do not do. The sermon ends on rock and sand: whoever hears and does is like a wise man building on stone; whoever hears and does not builds on sand, and the house falls. Do not read this as a ladder to climb in one day. Pick one verse — the Lord's prayer, the birds, the rock — and live it today.

days.label: Mark 4
days.devotional: Mark's fourth chapter is a day of teaching by the sea, in parables. A sower goes out, and the seed falls on four kinds of ground: the path, the rocks, the thorns, and the good soil. Jesus explains it privately: the word is the seed, and the ground is the hearer. Some never let it in; some receive it with joy and lose it when affliction comes; some let thorns — cares, riches, lusts — choke it; some bear fruit, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. Two more small parables follow: seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, and a mustard seed that becomes a great sheltering tree. The kingdom grows quietly, God giving the increase. Then evening comes, and theory becomes water. A great storm of wind rises; the waves beat into the ship till it is filling; Jesus sleeps on a pillow in the stern. 'Master, carest thou not that we perish?' He arises, rebukes the wind, and says unto the sea, 'Peace, be still.' There is a great calm, and the disciples ask the right question with trembling: 'What manner of man is this?' Put yourself in both scenes today — which soil are you, and which storm is yours? The sower is still sowing, and the sleeper in the stern still holds the sea.

days.label: Matthew 13
days.devotional: Jesus teaches the mysteries of the kingdom in parables by the sea again — this time Matthew collects seven. The sower with its four soils, then the wheat and the tares growing together until the harvest, the mustard seed, the leaven hidden in three measures of meal, the treasure hidden in a field, the pearl of great price, and the net drawing in every kind of fish. Two threads run through all of them. First, the kingdom is small and quiet now — seed, leaven, a tiny pearl — but its end is certain: harvest, separation, a treasure kept. Second, the kingdom is worth everything: the man sells all he has for the field; the merchant sells everything for the pearl. 'Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.' Notice that — for joy. The cost is not gritted teeth; it is a glad trade. Ask yourself honestly: what have I actually given up for this treasure, and what am I still holding back? The harvest is patient, but it is coming.

days.label: John 6
days.devotional: John 6 begins with bread and ends with bread of a different kind. Five thousand follow Jesus to a mountain; a lad has five barley loaves and two small fishes; Jesus gives thanks, distributes, and everyone eats as much as they want. Twelve baskets of fragments remain — more left over than the boy started with. The crowd wants to make him a king, but he withdraws, walks on the sea in the dark ('It is I; be not afraid'), and the next day teaches them what the miracle meant. 'Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life.' The manna in the wilderness fed for a day; the Father now gives the true bread from heaven. 'I am that bread of life... I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever.' Many disciples find the saying hard and walk away. Jesus turns to the twelve: 'Will ye also go away?' And Peter answers for anyone who has tasted it: 'Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.' Two questions from this chapter: are you following the bread, or the Giver of it?

days.label: Luke 15
days.devotional: Three stories, one complaint. The Pharisees and scribes mutter, 'This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them,' and Jesus answers with a sheep, a coin, and a son. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine in the wilderness to find one lost sheep, and carries it home on his shoulders rejoicing. A woman lights a candle and sweeps the house until she finds one piece of silver, and calls her neighbours to rejoice with her. Then the longest story: a younger son demands his inheritance, spends it far away, and comes home broke — feeding pigs and dreaming of their husks. But while he is yet a great way off, his father sees him — he has been watching that road — and runs, and kisses him, and before any apology is finished calls for the robe, the ring, the shoes, and the fatted calf: 'For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.' The elder brother stands outside, refusing to go in, angry that grace was spent so freely on someone else. The chapter never says whether he entered. Which brother are you nearer today — the one carried home, or the one sulking at the door? The father goes out to both.

days.label: John 11
days.devotional: Jesus hears that Lazarus is sick and stays two more days where he is. To the disciples it looks like negligence; to Jesus it is appointment: 'This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God.' By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been dead four days, and both sisters have said the same sentence: 'Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.' Martha still believes — 'whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee' — and Jesus tells her plainly, 'I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.' At the grave, Jesus weeps. The shortest verse in the Gospels is also one of the deepest: he does not weep because he lacks a plan, but because death grieves him even when he is about to break it. Then, in a loud voice: 'Lazarus, come forth.' And he that was dead came forth. Notice what Jesus does not rush — the tears, the timing, the conversation with the sisters. Grief and glory share this chapter. If you are in a four-day waiting place today, the delay is not the end of the story.

days.label: Matthew 17
days.devotional: Six days after Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God — and after the first hard announcement of the cross — Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up into a high mountain apart. And he is transfigured before them: his face shines like the sun, his clothing white as the light. Moses and Elijah appear, talking with him — the Law and the Prophets, meeting their fulfillment. Peter, always quickest to speak, offers three tabernacles, 'not knowing what he said.' Then a bright cloud overshadows them, and a voice says what it said at the Jordan: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.' The disciples fall on their faces, sore afraid, until Jesus touches them: 'Arise, and be not afraid.' Coming down the mountain, they find the other nine unable to help an afflicted boy, and Jesus heals what faith as small as a grain of mustard seed could have moved. Glory on the mountain, need in the valley — and the same Lord in both. Notice the command: not behold him, but hear him. What has he said lately that you have not yet obeyed?

days.label: John 13
days.devotional: The night before the cross, Jesus knows three things — that his hour is come, that the Father has given all things into his hands, and that he is come from God and goes to God. What he does with omnipotence in hand is wash feet. He rises from supper, lays aside his garments, takes a towel, girds himself, pours water, and washes the disciples' feet — including the feet of the man who will betray him. Peter protests — 'Thou shalt never wash my feet' — and then overcorrects: 'not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.' Jesus quietly teaches him: you are clean; this is an example. 'If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.' Then comes the new commandment, given on the last night: 'That ye love one another, as I have loved you... By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples.' Love measured not by feelings but by towels and basins, by serving people who do not deserve it and will not notice. One test for today: is there a foot you have refused to wash — a task beneath you, a person too difficult? He already washed that one.

days.label: John 14
days.devotional: 'Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.' Jesus says it to men whose world is collapsing within hours, and he spends the chapter rebuilding its foundations. Troubled about the way? 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.' Troubled about seeing the Father? 'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.' Troubled about prayer? 'Whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do.' Troubled about being left? 'I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.' The Father and the Son make their home with the one who loves and obeys; the Comforter, the Holy Ghost, will teach all things and bring Christ's words to remembrance. And over all stands the promise that holds the rest: 'Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.' Notice that Jesus does not promise the absence of trouble — the next chapter opens with tribulation — but his own peace inside it. Name your trouble to him today, and take the gift he names: peace, not as the world gives.

days.label: Luke 22
days.devotional: The Passover arrives, and Jesus eats it with the twelve. 'With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer,' he says, and takes bread and the cup: 'This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.' Then, before the garden, he settles a dispute among them about who is greatest: 'he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; I am among you as he that serveth.' He warns Peter that Satan has desired to sift him as wheat — 'but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not.' In Gethsemane the scene strips everything away: 'Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.' An angel strengthens him; he prays more earnestly; his sweat is as great drops of blood. The disciples sleep, sorrowing. Then Judas arrives with a kiss and a crowd, and Peter's sword cuts off an ear that Jesus heals on the spot. Read the whole night in one sitting: the table, the dispute, the warning, the prayer, the kiss. Obedience here is not serene — it is sweat and 'nevertheless.' That is what love looks like when it costs.

days.label: John 18
days.devotional: Jesus crosses the brook Cedron into the garden, and Judas arrives with soldiers and lanterns. Jesus steps forward — 'Whom seek ye?' — and when they say, Jesus of Nazareth, he answers, 'I am he,' and they go backward and fall to the ground. The arrest happens on his terms: 'the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?' Peter draws a sword and cuts off Malchus's ear; Jesus heals it and stops the fight. What follows is three examinations, and in all of them Jesus tells the truth while everyone else manages it. Before Annas and Caiaphas he answers simply; a servant strikes him, and he answers the blow with a question. Before Pilate he says, 'My kingdom is not of this world... for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth,' and Pilate asks the question of every age and walks away without the answer: 'What is truth?' Meanwhile Peter, warming himself at the fire, denies him three times, exactly as foretold. The contrast is the sermon: the Lord who owns every word, and the disciple who loses his. Both stand in the same courtyard. Which will you be this week?

days.label: John 19
days.devotional: John's crucifixion account is strangely calm, told by the disciple who stood there. Jesus is scourged, crowned with thorns, and presented to the crowd: 'Behold the man!' Pilate keeps trying to release him; the crowd shouts crucify, and says the fatal thing, 'We have no king but Caesar.' Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, with a title Pilate wrote and would not change: JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS — written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. From the cross come the shortest, greatest sentences: 'Woman, behold thy son' — caring for his mother as he dies. 'I thirst.' 'It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.' Finished — completed, paid, accomplished — not a life cut short but a work completed. A soldier pierces his side, and blood and water come out. Two secret disciples, Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus, finally step forward to bury him with myrrh and aloes in a new sepulchre. Stand at the cross a while today without hurrying. The words 'It is finished' are addressed to you: nothing of the price is left unpaid, and nothing of your sin is left uncarried.

days.label: Matthew 28
days.devotional: The women come at dawn to see the sepulchre, carrying spices and grief. An earthquake meets them; an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it — not to let Jesus out, but to let everyone in. 'I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified. He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.' They run to tell the disciples 'with fear and great joy,' and meet Jesus himself on the road; they hold his feet and worship him. The guards are bribed to say the disciples stole the body while they slept — Matthew notes the story was still circulating when he wrote. Then the eleven meet him on a mountain in Galilee, and worship, 'but some doubted' — Matthew is honest about the room. Jesus answers doubt not with a lecture but with a commission: 'All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations... and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.' He is risen, as he said. Whatever you doubted last week, he answers the same way he answered theirs: with presence, and with work to do.

days.label: Luke 24
days.devotional: The last chapter of Luke is a series of meetings in one day. Two disciples walk to Emmaus, rehearsing their disappointment — 'we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel.' A stranger joins them, opens the Scriptures beginning at Moses and all the prophets, and stays for supper. At bread broken and blessed, 'their eyes were opened, and they knew him' — and he vanishes out of their sight. 'Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?' They rise and run back to Jerusalem that same night, and while they are still talking, Jesus stands in the midst of them: 'Peace be unto you.' They are terrified; he shows them his hands and his feet, and eats broiled fish — resurrection with a body, not a ghost. Then he opens their understanding: 'Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day: and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations.' He leads them out to Bethany, lifts his hands, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven. They return to the temple praising and blessing God. Notice: their hearts burned before their eyes opened. Sometimes understanding follows the road and the supper, not the other way round.

days.label: John 20
days.devotional: Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it is yet dark, finds the stone taken away, and runs for Peter and John. They race, look in, see the linen clothes lying and the napkin folded 'in a place by itself,' and believe — for as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again. But Mary stays weeping, and meets the risen Lord without recognizing him until he says one word: 'Mary.' She turns and says, Rabboni. That evening, the doors shut for fear of the Jews, Jesus stands among them: 'Peace be unto you,' shows them his hands and his side, breathes on them, and says, 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost.' Thomas is absent, and will not believe without touching. Eight days later the doors are shut again, and Jesus comes again — straight to Thomas: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands.' Thomas answers with the highest confession in the Gospel: 'My Lord and my God.' Jesus then blesses all who will believe without seeing — 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.' John tells us why he wrote the book: 'these are written, that ye might believe... and that believing ye might have life through his name.' That blessing is for the reader. That is you.

days.label: John 21
days.devotional: Afterward, by the sea of Tiberias, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a figure on the shore says, cast the net on the right side of the ship — and the net fills with one hundred and fifty-three great fishes, and none of them dares ask, Who art thou? knowing it is the Lord. Breakfast on coals, bread, and fish follows, the third appearance John records. Then comes the scene every restoration needs: Jesus asks Peter three times, 'Lovest thou me?' — matching the three denials — and gives him a job each time: 'Feed my lambs... Feed my sheep.' Peter is not demoted for his failure; he is commissioned. Jesus goes on to describe the kind of death by which Peter will glorify God, and Peter immediately asks about John. Jesus' answer is a gift to every comparer: 'What is that to thee? follow thou me.' John closes his Gospel with characteristic honesty: if everything were written, the world could not contain the books. Three weeks end here, at a charcoal fire, with a failed man re-hired. The question Jesus leaves with you is Peter's: not what happened to your failures, but 'Lovest thou me?' Answer it, and then follow.
